newsitem.title: USA: Dow turnaround sends dollar to highs by U.S. close.
newsitem.headline: Dow turnaround sends dollar to highs by U.S. close.

text.p: The dollar ended at session highs against the mark and yen on Monday, buoyed by an impressive turnaround in U.S. stocks and remarks from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp.

After tumbling 247 points to end at 7695 on Friday -- the second largest single-day point loss total on record -- the Dow Jones Industrials battled back from early losses to end up over 100 points on Monday.
The dollar, which had fallen in tandem with stocks for much of last week, rose as the blue chip index turned positive and gathered steam in afternoon trading.
"We really traded in lock-step with the Dow for much of the day," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.
The Dow ended the day up 109 points at 7803, a near-200 point turnaround from its session lows.
The dollar edged up to 1.8344/49 marks from 1.8200/10 at the open. It also rose to end at 118.04/09 yen from 117.90/00.
Helping the dollar were remarks from the Bundesbank's Hans-Juergen Krupp, who said on Monday that a rise in German interest rates at the present time would be "very damaging" to the German economy.
Krupp added that recent mark weakness was worrisome, but said he saw little evidence that the weaker currency was fuelling inflation.

Although jitters over prospects for German action on interest rates had subsided as the dollar came off its highs against the mark last week, the comments lent dollar/mark a solid bid before the recovery in stocks.

"The comments highlight the fact that Germany's economy is not running away and that they are not importing inflation so there is no real reason to hike rates," said Robert Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.

Sales of marks for yen kept dollar/yen gains in check after Japanese trade data supported the rate in overseas dealings. Mark/yen ended the day at a session low of 64.44, down from an earlier peak of 64.91.
The Japanese Ministry of Finance reported that Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus climbed 70 percent in July to 849 billion yen -- less than some analysts had feared.
Dealers said the figures soothed fears that trade tensions between the United States and Japan could soon escalate.
Dollar activity was kept in check on Monday by caution ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting on Tuesday and key U.S. trade data for June, due on Wednesday.
Economists polled by Reuters were unanimous in predicting no change in policy at the Fed's regularly scheduled confab.
Despite last week's sharp losses, traders remained positive about the dollar's prospects, citing an encouraging bounce from key support at 1.8050 in dollar/mark and a subsequent climb.

"There is a tendency to think of this as a correction rather than a turnaround in the market and I think that's justified," said Bob Savage, chief dealer at Lehman Brothers, referring to the recent downturn.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar rose to 1.5170/80 Swiss francs from 1.5091/96 at the open, and edged up to Canadian $1.3882/87 from C$1.3872/77.
The British pound slipped to $1.6038/43 from $1.6060/70 at the outset of trading, while the Australian dollar fell to $0.7379/84 from $0.7400/10.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
